item.title: Limbic network hyperconnectivity, fasting appetite hormone dysregulation and impaired go/no-go performance in youths with bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BJPsych open
Bipolar disorder in youths is associated with metabolic dysregulation, impaired inhibitory control and limbic network connectivity changes. To investigate whether limbic network connectivity is associated with appetite hormones and inhibitory control in youths with bipolar disorder. The current study included 68 youths with bipolar disorder and 57 age- and gender-matched controls. They completed clinical assessments, the go/no-go (GNG) task, fasting appetite hormone (leptin, adiponectin, insulin and ghrelin) tests and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Region of interest (ROI)-to-ROI functional connectivity was analysed across 17 limbic ROIs. Cluster-level inferences were derived by using threshold-free cluster enhancement with family-wise error correction (p < 0.05). Furthermore, associations with appetite hormones and GNG task parameters were investigated. Compared with the control individuals, youths with bipolar disorder exhibited elevated leptin (p = 0.005) and insulin levels (p < 0.001), poorer performance on the GNG task and hyperconnectivity within the limbic network, identifying a significant cluster comprising the right anterior parahippocampal gyrus (aPHG)-right thalamus and right aPHG-hypothalamus edges (cluster-level family-wise error-corrected p = 0.045). No significant correlations were observed between limbic hyperconnectivity, appetite hormone levels and GNG task performance. Current cross-sectional cohort indicates that youths with bipolar disorder exhibit concurrent alterations in appetite hormones, inhibitory control and limbic connectivity. These findings provide a characterisation of youth bipolar disorder across multiple indices, although longitudinal studies are necessary to understand how these features relate to long-term clinical trajectories.

item.title: Expertise modifies neural responses to causal inference during language comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Linguistic communication relies on shared common ground, yet different individuals in a community have specialized semantic knowledge. As a key example, physicians acquire rich knowledge about the causes of illness. An open question is whether such "causal expertise" influences the neural basis of language comprehension. Here we tested the hypothesis that when understanding everyday language like, "Holly used a grimy faucet during her overseas plane ride. Now she has the stomach flu," medical experts retrieve richer representations in semantic networks of the brain. Physicians (n=16) and age- and education-matched controls (n=16) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences about illness or object mechanics as well as control vignettes that did not elicit causal inferences. Vignettes were linguistically matched across conditions and were accessible to experts and non-experts alike. Across both groups, causal vignettes about illness engaged a temporoparietal semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, i.e., people and animals (precuneus and left temporoparietal junction), whereas causal vignettes about object mechanics engaged a semantic network associated with places and objects. Critically, physicians' responses in the animacy network were more robust and self-similar, suggesting the activation of richer semantic knowledge. Medical expertise effects were specific to biological inferences rather than mechanical or mental state inferences. By contrast, individually localized frontotemporal language and frontoparietal reasoning networks did not respond preferentially to causally connected sentences or show effects of expertise. Our findings suggest that causal expertise alters neural responses to causal inferences that unfold automatically during language comprehension.

item.title: An orthographic advantage in spoken word recognition: Behavioral and ERP evidence from cross- and within-modal priming in Korean
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Spoken word recognition may benefit from orthographic information even when spelling differs from surface pronunciation. Korean Hangul preserves spelling across regular phonological changes, allowing us to compare primes matching a target’s written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U). We report two EEG experiments with independent participant groups, using primed auditory lexical decision on the same 120 disyllabic Korean targets, with within-modal auditory primes (Experiment 1) and cross-modal visual primes (Experiment 2). In both experiments, O primes shortened response latencies and improved accuracy relative to U primes, and produced greater behavioral benefits than P primes. The O–P latency advantage was larger with visual than auditory primes. Phonological latency priming was modest with auditory primes and was not established with visual primes, whereas evidence favored no between-experiment difference in orthographic latency priming. Orthographic relatedness was associated with more positive centro-parietal amplitudes in the N400 window (350–550 ms) in both experiments, without clear evidence of a between-experiment difference. Following visual primes, it also increased fronto-central positivity in the 250–350 ms window, more than following auditory primes. The predicted P200 enhancement was not reliably established. The behavioral O–P advantage was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference. The findings suggest that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation and support a role for orthographic relations in spoken word recognition.

item.title: Brain Tissue Proportionality and General Cognitive Ability Across Three Adult Cohorts
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract General cognitive ability may relate to the proportional allocation of brain tissue beyond overall tissue volume. We examined five FreeSurfer compartments using compositional data analysis: cortical gray matter, cerebral white matter, subcortical gray matter, total cerebellum, and brainstem. Human Connectome Project Young Adult data (HCP-YA; N = 1,101) provided discovery estimates; the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study (DLBS; N = 418) and Amsterdam Open MRI Collection ID1000 (AOMIC; N = 926) provided independent cohort tests. Four isometric log-ratio coordinates represented composition, with age, sex, and log total analyzed tissue volume included separately. Composition explained additional cognitive variance in DLBS (partial R² = 4.20%, p = .00154) and AOMIC (partial R² = 1.35%, p = .014). The total-cerebellum-to-cerebral-white-matter contrast selected in HCP was positive in both replication cohorts: standardized β = 0.162 (heteroskedasticity-robust 95% confidence interval 0.072–0.252) in DLBS and 0.097 (0.024–0.170) in AOMIC. Participant-pairs bootstrap intervals supported both associations. Replacing total tissue volume with estimated intracranial volume attenuated the AOMIC association, whereas including both preserved it. Relative macroanatomical allocation is associated with broad cognitive ability conditional on analyzed tissue volume, with differing effect magnitudes across cohorts. These cross-sectional findings do not establish causal tissue trade-offs.

item.title: Emotion knowledge is structured in a grid-like coordinate system in the human ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. Although this circumplex organization has shaped decades of research, its neural implementation remains unclear. Here, we asked whether abstract emotion concepts are encoded using grid-like coordinate principles in the human brain. During fMRI, participants tracked trajectories through affective space conveyed through morphs of facial expressions and sequences of phrases. We found that ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) encoded affective space with robust hexadirectional modulation characteristic of grid-like coding. This coordinate representation generalized across stimulus modalities, indicating abstraction beyond perceptual features. The grid-like signal reflected a metric organization of emotion concepts independent of overt behavior, whereas distance-related signals in vmPFC predicted trial-by-trial affective judgements. Together, these findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain that can support predictive inference and flexible decision-making.

item.title: Animal fluency networks and item-based trajectories in people with Parkinson's disease before and after deep brain stimulation surgery.
item.description:
Journal of neuropsychology
Consistent decline in animal fluency occurs in people with Parkinson's disease (PD) post-surgery for Deep Brain Stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus (STN-DBS). Recent findings indicate that patients produce fewer words after (vs. before) surgery. Also, they produce smaller clusters of related animals, fewer switches between clusters, and more frequent (lexical frequency) and earlier-acquired words. In this paper, we further investigated difficulties in lexical retrieval by reporting on word networks (to study the structure of the mental lexicon) and item-based trajectories (to understand how the linguistic characteristics of the task change as the task progresses) of 61 Dutch-speaking individuals diagnosed with PD before and post-surgery for STN-DBS and 40 age and education-matched healthy controls. Word networks contained a higher number of edges and nodes for healthy controls relative to people with PD post-surgery (adjusting for differences in sample size). Also, patients before surgery produced a network with a lower cluster coefficient relative to healthy controls, as well as to people with PD post-surgery. Item-based trajectories showed that both healthy controls and people with PD produced words of increasing complexity as they proceed with the task (e.g., less frequent, acquired later, of higher length). Also, healthy controls showed a steeper increase in the age of acquisition of words across the first ten responses compared to PD post-surgery. The re-emergence of structure (clustering) in word networks post-surgery for STN-DBS and the differences in item-based trajectories (vs. healthy controls) represent novel markers of lexical retrieval that are affected by surgery for STN-DBS and PD.

item.title: Regional lesion burden and chronic post-stroke aphasia severity: Incremental value beyond total lesion volume.
item.description:
Applied neuropsychology. Adult
We examined whether regional lesion burden adds information beyond clinical variables and total lesion volume regarding chronic aphasia severity. This secondary analysis of the Aphasia Recovery Cohort included 195 participants with left-hemisphere stroke, Western Aphasia Battery Aphasia Quotient (AQ) ≤93.8, and assessment ≥180 days after stroke. Lesion burden was quantified in five atlas-defined groups. Partial Spearman correlations were adjusted for age at stroke, sex, time to assessment, and lesion volume, and four ridge-regression models were compared using 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation. A sensitivity analysis included participants whose imaging and Western Aphasia Battery assessments were ≤90 days apart (n = 128). Dorsal white-matter burden remained associated with lower AQ after adjustment (partial ρ = -0.261; false-discovery-rate q = 0.002). Adding regional burdens to the clinical-plus-volume model increased mean cross-validated R2 from 0.306 to 0.384 (ΔR2 = 0.078) and reduced mean absolute error from 18.76 to 17.31 AQ points. In the time-restricted sample, R2 increased from 0.312 to 0.442 (ΔR2 = 0.130), with the dorsal association persisting (partial ρ = -0.307). Regional lesion burden adds information beyond lesion volume and supports anatomical characterization of chronic aphasia severity.

item.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex modulates single-neuron activity in humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is an established treatment for depression, yet the fundamental question of how cortical stimulation influences single neurons in deep brain circuits critical for mood regulation remains unanswered. Using a rare opportunity to record from intracranial microelectrodes while TMS was delivered in four neurosurgical patients, we evaluated the responses of 185 single neurons. Artifact cleaning enabled single-neuron spikes to be resolved as early as 8 ms after stimulation. We found that single-pulse TMS to the left dlPFC elicited time-locked firing responses in 46% of neurons (26% facilitated only, 19% suppressed only, 1% both). These responses occurred within deep bilateral cortical and subcortical structures, including the putamen and thalamus. Single-pulse TMS tended to facilitate spiking in striato-thalamic putative inhibitory neurons from ~8 ms, peaking at ~80 to 100 ms, and decaying until ~600 ms. In contrast, putative excitatory neurons and limbic areas were suppressed with a slower time course lasting to ~1,000 ms. TMS-evoked potentials recorded from intracranial depth macroelectrodes to quantify network activity revealed that the modulation of responsive neurons was positively correlated with cortico-striato-thalamic network activity and anticorrelated with limbic network activity in one participant with sufficient network and unit sampling. These results suggest that dlPFC TMS recruits a high percentage of neurons spanning cortical and subcortical brain regions bilaterally. The recruitment pattern selectively involves increasing the firing rate of inhibitory neurons in executive control networks while suppressing limbic excitatory drive, providing a candidate cellular mechanism for how cortical stimulation modulates distributed brain networks.

item.title: A causal account of the neural origins of mental fatigue.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Successful goal-directed behavior often requires the exertion of effortful cognitive control processes, but it remains unclear why engaging in cognitive control is experienced as effortful and induces fatigue. Here, we tested the hypothesis that sustained activation in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC)-a neural substrate of cognitive control-causally induces motivational fatigue via the accumulation of prefrontal glutamate metabolites. For this purpose, we combined brain stimulation with spectroscopy imaging to assess how increasing DLPFC excitability during an effortful mental task changes the motivation for mental effort and glutamate concentrations. We found that stimulating the DLPFC during mental effort exertion improved mental performance at the cost of increased posteffort motivational fatigue, suggesting a causal role of DLPFC activation for inducing fatigue. On the neural level, DLPFC activation during effortful cognition also increased prefrontal concentrations of glutamate, which statistically explained the fatigue-induced lower motivation for mental effort. A corresponding analysis of combined glutamate-glutamine (Glx) concentrations revealed converging effects. Together, these findings provide causal evidence that enhanced DLPFC activation contributes to fatigue via neurochemical changes, supporting neuro-metabolic accounts of fatigue and offering new insights into why demanding cognitive tasks are perceived as effortful.

item.title: Associations between nonfatal strangulation-related brain injury in intimate partner violence and resting-state functional connectivity.
item.description:
Neuropsychology
Examine the association between nonfatal strangulation-related probable brain injury (NFS-BI), resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC), and verbal memory, among females who experienced physical intimate partner violence (IPV). Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging was analyzed for 110 females aged 18-60 years who experienced physical IPV. rsFC was characterized by seven graph theory metrics across three brain parcellation atlases (Power, Seitzman, and Schaefer-456 Parcellation[4S]). Responses to the Brain Injury Screening Questionnaire determined IPV-head trauma frequency, experience of probable NFS-BI, and other/additional non-IPV and IPV-related BI. Verbal memory was characterized by three measures from the California Verbal Learning Test, Third Edition: (a) Long Delay, Free Recall, (b) Trials 1-5 correct index scores, and (c) memory retention from Trials 1-5 to Long Delay, Free Recall. NFS-BI was significantly associated with reductions in within-default mode network (DMN) connectivity (Power: B = -0.03, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -0.03, p = .005; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .03), DMN segregation (Power: B = -0.04, p = .006; Seitzman: B = -0.04, p = .007; 4S: B = -0.03, p = .02), and global modularity (Power: B = -0.01, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -0.02, p = .008; 4S: B = -0.02, p = .007). Interactions between NFS-BI and within-DMN strength (Power: B = -150.05, p = .03; Seitzman: B = -212.11 p = .01; 4S: B = -204.52, p = .002), DMN segregation (Power: B = -106.97, p = .02; Seitzman: B = -114.54 p = .008; 4S: B = -189.88, p < .001), and modularity (Power: B = -373.80, p = .003; Seitzman: B = -367.35, p = .001; 4S: B = -312.55, p = .006) were significantly associated with memory retention. Those who experienced probable NFS-BI demonstrated altered rsFC compared with those who did not. Interactions between DMN rsFC and NFS-BI were significantly associated with memory retention. Future work should assess individuals with NFS-BI longitudinally to understand its effects on long-term brain health. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

item.title: State-Dependent EEG Markers of Excitation/Inhibition and Hemodynamic State Are Associated with Random Noise Stimulation Effects.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Non-invasive brain stimulation effects vary substantially across individuals, yet the physiological factors associated with this variability remain unclear. We tested whether baseline and task-related EEG markers of excitation/inhibition (E/I) and hemodynamic state are associated with the effects of transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) on learning. Participants completed a mathematical learning task during active or sham tRNS. We indexed E/I-related population dynamics using the EEG aperiodic exponent, for which lower values have been linked to relatively greater excitation than inhibition, and assessed hemodynamic state using fNIRS-derived oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO). Behavioral learning was modeled using generalized linear mixed-effects models. tRNS accelerated learning relative to sham stimulation but did not reliably induce pre-post changes in resting-state aperiodic exponent or HbO. Instead, stimulation effects were state-dependent. Higher resting-state aperiodic exponent and lower resting-state HbO were associated with greater behavioral gains under tRNS, while task-related aperiodic exponent was associated with stimulation-related differences in learning. Task-evoked HbO was associated with learning rate but did not significantly differentiate stimulation effects. Across modalities, the findings identify complementary electrophysiological and hemodynamic correlates of variability in learning under stimulation. However, statistical support for the EEG moderation effects was attenuated in models including participant-specific learning slopes, indicating sensitivity to random-effects specification and the need for replication. The findings argue against a simple tonic-shift account of tRNS and support a state-dependent framework in which stimulation effects depend on ongoing electrophysiological and hemodynamic context. EEG and fNIRS provided complementary information about variability in learning and stimulation response, supporting multimodal approaches to understanding and individualizing neuromodulation.

item.title: Do autistic traits modulate the neural processing of logical rule violations in visual and auditory modalities?
item.description:
NeuroImage
Similarities in cognitive processing have been reported between individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and non-clinical individuals with autistic traits. However, previous research on autistic traits has primarily focused on social-emotional domains, with limited attention to abstract logical reasoning. Given that sensitivity to rules and patterns is a notable characteristic of the autism spectrum, logical rule processing may be particularly informative for understanding cognitive differences associated with autistic traits. The present research aimed to investigate the behavioral and neural responses of students with autistic traits to logical and illogical number sequences through two event-related potential studies. Based on Autism Spectrum Quotient-10 (AQ-10) scores, participants were categorized into High-AQ and Low-AQ groups. In Study 1, both groups judged whether visually presented logical and illogical three number sequences followed a logical incremental rule. In Study 2, both groups performed the same task as in Study 1, except number sequences were presented in the auditory modality. No significant group difference was found in response to logical number sequences in either study. However, relative to the Low-AQ group, the High-AQ group exhibited larger P2 and P3 amplitudes and more negative emotional reactions to illogical number sequences in the visual modality (Study 1), and more positive N1 and LPP amplitudes, and higher arousal ratings to illogical number sequences in the auditory modality (Study 2). These findings suggest that students with autistic traits may exhibit altered neural responses and heightened emotional reactivity specifically to stimuli that violate logical rules in separate visual and auditory studies.

item.title: Same Networks, Different Dynamics: Parsimony in Auditory Cognitive Task Processing.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Distinct cognitive states might be supported either by dedicated, task-specific brain networks or by flexible modulation within shared ones, a distinction central to understanding how the brain allocates neural resources. Guided by the principle of parsimony, we hypothesized that both language and numerical cognition, when matched for sensory modality and attentional demand, would engage a common network architecture differentiated primarily through targeted modulation of connectivity strength and temporal dynamics rather than wholesale reconfiguration. We applied a jackknife-based dynamic functional connectivity approach to examine time-varying network engagement during auditory language comprehension and auditory math problem-solving in 172 age- and sex-matched participants from the Human Connectome Project-Young Adult cohort, using the Desikan-Killiany atlas and an 85% participation threshold. Of the significant connections identified, many were retained across both tasks, with 87 connections common to story and math, compared with 26 story-associated and 11 math-associated connections. Rather than indicating a novel shared-core architecture, this overlap is consistent with prior evidence that task functional connectivity is strongly constrained by a common intrinsic connectivity backbone. We therefore used the shared edge set as a common network framework for testing how two modality-matched, but cognitively distinct auditory tasks differ in connectivity strength and temporal variability. Among the 87 shared connections, 84 showed significant task-related differences in mean connectivity strength, indicating that story-math differentiation was expressed primarily through quantitative modulation of shared connections rather than wholesale changes in edge membership. Exploratory rolling-correlation analyses further suggested that some edges may show temporal variability in math-story connectivity correspondence even when mean connectivity strength is similar, highlighting a potential dynamic feature not captured by static connectivity estimates alone. Together, these findings suggest that story and math processing rely on a broadly shared connectivity backbone, while task differentiation emerges through graded modulation of connection strength and, in some cases, temporal variability.

item.title: Integrating neuroplasticity into whole-brain modeling: From synapses to neural populations.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
The brain's ability to learn, adapt, and recover hinges on synaptic plasticity, yet most large-scale neural models overlook this core feature. In this review, we argue that embedding plasticity is essential for the simulation of realistic population-level brain activity. To this end, we explore specific computational attempts at scaling microscopic single-neuron plasticity rules to mesoscopic populations, drawing from mechanistic insights into short-term synaptic dynamics, long-term potentiation, and homeostatic regulation. We also discuss how plasticity mechanisms in neural field and neural mass models can potentially help us understand recovery trajectories, and how dysfunctional plasticity can play a role in them. Finally, we review state-of-the-art multiscale co-simulations methods that bridge spiking neuron networks with neural field and mass models and discuss their ability to link microscopic synaptic mechanisms with macroscopic brain dynamics. By embedding plasticity as a core feature, we can develop mean-field models that are more realistic and powerful tools for understanding brain function and recovery.

item.title: Superior Frontal Gyrus Cortical Thickness Mediates the Association Between Openness to Experience and Theory of Mind: Evidence from the Human Connectome Project
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Theory of mind (ToM), the capacity to infer the mental states of others, varies considerably across healthy adults. Openness to experience has been linked both to social-cognitive abilities and to thinner prefrontal cortex, but whether cortical structure statistically accounts for the association between openness and ToM is unknown. We tested whether bilateral superior frontal gyrus (SFG) cortical thickness mediates this association. Methods: Data from 1,049 healthy young adults with complete data were drawn from the Human Connectome Project. ToM was indexed by accuracy on the Heider-Simmel social animation task, openness by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and SFG thickness by FreeSurfer. Models adjusted for age, sex, intracranial volume and fluid intelligence; indirect effects were tested with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied. Results: Openness showed a positive total effect on ToM accuracy (beta = .081, p = .009). Higher openness was associated with thinner left and right SFG (beta = -.085 and -.084), and thinner SFG with higher ToM accuracy (beta = -.082 and -.075). Indirect effects were significant (left: .0069, 95% CI [.0010, .0158]; right: .0063, 95% CI [.0007, .0146]), accounting for approximately 8.5% and 7.8% of the total effect, and remained significant after rank-based normalisation of the ceiling-affected ToM scores. Conclusions: SFG cortical thickness partially and statistically mediates the association between openness to experience and social cognition. Because the data are cross-sectional and effects are small, the findings do not establish a causal mechanism, neural efficiency or synaptic pruning, but they identify a candidate structural pathway for longitudinal testing.

item.title: Human iEEG recordings during audiovisual speech violations support and extend predictive routing models
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Rather than constantly reconstructing the world solely through sensory input, predictive processing theories posit that the brain utilizes predictions maintained as internal representations to guide sensory processing. An emerging model, predictive routing, proposes that an interplay between neuronal gamma (40-150 Hz) and alpha-beta (10-30 Hz) rhythms implements a dynamic mechanism for predictive processing. Namely, predictions enhance alpha-beta oscillations that suppress gamma activity during the processing of predicted inputs. While this model is supported by animal studies, its validity has not been fully explored within the human brain. The present study addresses this by leveraging human intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings across superior temporal and prefrontal/premotor areas of seven presurgical epilepsy patients during an audiovisual speech paradigm. We calculated iEEG power in the theta, alpha-beta, and high gamma bands during simple auditory deviance, multisensory integration, and a condition where an incongruent visual cue (lip movements) clashed with an auditory stimulus (a syllable), creating audiovisual incongruence that can elicit the McGurk illusion. Results revealed increased high-gamma and decreased alpha-beta power in the superior temporal cortex in response to auditory deviance and the McGurk condition, while frontal areas, despite reflecting a similar decrease in alpha-beta power, did not present this high gamma prediction error signal. Instead, the theta band revealed a strong prediction error signal in the McGurk condition, consistent with theories on the role of theta in reorganizing cortical networks. These results both support and extend existing predictive routing models for human-specific forms of predictive processing.

item.title: State-independent functional connectomic architecture captures transdiagnostic network alterations and clinical variation
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Psychiatric disorders show substantial overlap across diagnostic categories while differing markedly in clinical expression. Whether these shared abnormalities and individual differences are embedded in stable functional brain architecture rather than in state-specific connectivity remains unclear. Methods: We integrated functional connectomes across one resting-state and six task-based fMRI conditions in 377 participants from the YaleNeuroConnect cohort, including 223 healthy controls and 154 individuals with psychiatric disorders. Principal component analysis was applied to each participant's functional connectivity data across the seven states to derive a state-independent connectivity representation. Network-based statistics then identified components showing significant case-control differences. Cross-state consistency was assessed, and findings were validated in an independent UCLA cohort of 177 participants. Associations between component expression and clinical measures were further examined within the Yale psychiatric group. Results: Cross-paradigm connectivity revealed two reproducible patterns of state-independent network alteration. One pattern showed reduced connectivity among limbic, somatomotor and salience systems, whereas the other showed stronger cerebellar coupling with limbic and somatomotor systems. Both patterns showed consistent case-control differences across functional states and generalized to an independent UCLA cohort. Their clinical relevance, however, differed. Greater expression of the cerebello-cortical connectivity pattern was associated with lower positive affect, greater psychopathology and more everyday executive difficulties, whereas the reduced limbic-somatomotor-salience connectivity pattern showed no significant clinical associations. Conclusions: These findings delineate a stable reorganization of large-scale functional architecture across psychiatric disorders and suggest that broadly expressed psychiatric abnormalities and individual clinical variation may be differentially represented within the altered connectome.

item.title: Frontoparietal functional connectivity underlies top-down attention in mild cognitive impairment
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment frequently show attention problems such as reduced top-down control, the ability to ignore task-irrelevant information. It is unclear whether this reduction corresponds with decreased brain connectivity. We aimed to determine whether and how differences in functional connectivity, or the correlated activity between brain areas, explain differences in top-down control in amnestic mild cognitive impairment. We conducted a case-control study with 26 patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (58-91 years; 10 women) and 29 age-matched healthy older adults (60-79 years; 9 women). All patients and control participants underwent neuropsychological assessment to confirm diagnosis and healthy cognitive status, respectively. We used resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging at 3T to analyse functional connectivity. Top-down control was estimated with a 'theory of visual attention'-based verbal partial-report task (parameter α ; higher α indicates poorer control). We identified visual and attention-relevant functional brain networks and tested for differences between patients and controls while controlling for age and gender. Compared with healthy control participants, patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment showed lower functional connectivity in the left frontoparietal attention network and in one visual network and worse top-down control α (t(37.43) = -2.24, p = 0.031). The reduced connectivity in the frontoparietal network, but not the visual network, significantly correlated with top-down control α across all participants (ρ = -0.33, p = 0.003) and in the patient group (ρ = -0.48, p = 0.014). Moreover, connectivity in the frontoparietal network mediated the relationship between amnestic mild cognitive impairment and top-down control α. These results link lower frontoparietal connectivity to worse attentional control in patients with amnestic mild cognitive impairment. Worse control reflects inefficient attentional selection and increasing distraction by irrelevant information during perceptual processing and encoding into working memory. Overall, this implicates a role for the frontoparietal network in maintaining cognitive control or, more generally, supporting cognitive functioning in older adults with emerging cognitive impairment.

item.title: Adaptive and maladaptive microstructural remodelling of the maternal brain revealed by diffusion kurtosis imaging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Postpartum depression (PPD) is a major maternal mental health concern that may arise during neurobiological and emotional adaptation. Alterations in these adaptive processes may contribute to depressive symptom vulnerability; however, the neurobiological basis of postpartum brain adaptation remains unclear. We investigated microstructural brain remodelling in postpartum women using diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI) and evaluated its association with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scores. We compared brain magnetic resonance imaging findings between 15 women one month postpartum and 10 nulliparous women without psychiatric disorders. Tract-based spatial statistics and regions of interest were analysed using diffusion tensor and kurtosis metrics. Compared with nulliparous women, postpartum women showed significantly lower mean and axial diffusivity values in white matter regions, including the frontal lobe, basal ganglia, and corticospinal tract. The posterior insular cortex showed increased mean and radial kurtosis, whereas the putamen demonstrated decreased diffusivity. EPDS scores showed positive correlations with kurtosis metrics in the amygdala and negative correlations with diffusivity metrics in the hypothalamus. These findings suggest that the postpartum brain undergoes coordinated microstructural remodelling involving emotional regulation, stress response, and maternal behavioural adaptations. Thus, DKI may provide an objective neuroimaging biomarker for identifying maladaptive postpartum brain changes associated with depressive symptoms.

item.title: Posterior cortical gray matter heterogeneity between hyposmia- and RBD-defined prodromal phenotypes in Parkinson's disease: a PPMI voxel-based morphometry study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD) includes clinically distinct enrollment phenotypes. We examined whole-brain gray matter volume (GMV) in Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) participants recruited through hyposmia-only or REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)-only pathways and assessed the stability of the findings. Methods Baseline T1-weighted MRI from 465 hyposmia-only and 149 RBD-only participants (N = 614) was analyzed with CAT12/SPM25 voxel-based morphometry (VBM). Models included age, sex, intracranial volume, and scanner family. Whole-brain clusters were defined at voxel p < 0.001 and tested using family-wise error (FWE) correction. We examined scanner-restricted samples, 123 sex/scanner-matched pairs, and 10,000-sign-flip permutation analysis of linear models (PALM). Bilateral cuneus/calcarine estimates and clinical assessments were exploratory. Results Whole-brain analysis identified a posterior phenotype effect (F cluster: k = 4,499; pFWE = 4.15×10⁻⁷), with higher GMV in hyposmia-only participants. In 123 matched pairs, a posterior H > RBD T cluster survived correction (pFWE = 0.0266), whereas the F contrast did not. PALM also identified a posterior effect (two-sided threshold-free cluster enhancement [TFCE] FWE p = 0.0027; voxelwise FWE p = 0.0277). Adjusted bilateral cuneus differences were + 0.211 mL (95% CI 0.095–0.327) in the full cohort and + 0.187 mL (0.041–0.333) after matching. MRI-proximal RBD screening questionnaire scores showed no significant association with regional GMV. Conclusions Posterior cortical GMV differed between these enrollment-defined prodromal phenotypes. The anatomical finding was supported by nonparametric inference, although the matched F test and strictest scanner restriction were nonsignificant. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish its clinical relevance.

item.title: Resting-State EEG Theta-Band Functional Connectivity Characterizes Heterogeneity in Internet Gaming Disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background. Symptom-based assessments capture IGD severity but provide limited information about neurophysiological heterogeneity. We examined whether resting-state EEG amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) profiles relate to IGD symptoms and reveal connectivity-defined heterogeneity. Methods. Thirty participants with IGD and thirty healthy controls underwent five-minute eyes-closed resting-state EEG. Source-level AEC was estimated across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Exploratory representational similarity analysis tested associations between connectivity-profile dissimilarity and IGD-20 differences; theta-AEC profiles within IGD were further examined using principal component analysis and k-means clustering. Results. Within IGD, theta-AEC dissimilarity was associated with mood-modification differences ( rₛ = 0.277, p FDR = 0.020), whereas the corresponding association in controls was not significant. Exploratory clustering indicated connectivity heterogeneity, with the largest difference involving Visual–Salience/Ventral Attention connectivity; clusters did not differ in IGD-20 scores or weekly gaming time. Conclusions. Theta-AEC may capture symptom-related neurophysiological variation within IGD.

item.title: Functional Connectivity Gradients Reveal Cortical Hierarchical Reorganization Across the Cirrhosis–Hepatic Encephalopathy Spectrum
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a common neurocognitive complication of cirrhosis, but how macroscale cortical hierarchy is reorganized across the cirrhosis–HE spectrum remains incompletely understood. We characterized functional connectome gradient alterations across clinically defined cirrhosis stages and examined their clinical correlates. Methods This cross-sectional study included 104 participants: 35 patients with HE, 33 with cirrhosis without HE (NHE), and 36 healthy controls. Resting-state functional MRI was used to derive the first three connectivity gradients (G1–G3). Group differences were assessed at global, network, and cortical-parcel levels, and associations with blood ammonia, liver disease severity, and cognition were examined in patients with cirrhosis. Results Both NHE and HE showed reduced G1 range and variance versus healthy controls, indicating compression of the sensorimotor-to-transmodal hierarchy. Both groups showed higher somatomotor G1 and lower control and default mode G1, whereas HE additionally showed lower limbic G1. The only significant HE–NHE parcel-level difference involved the right temporal pole. Higher ammonia was associated with higher somatomotor G1 and lower control and default mode G1, while greater liver disease severity was associated mainly with lower limbic and default mode G1. Poorer cognition showed broadly corresponding associations. G2 and G3 did not differ among groups, and the main findings remained robust in sensitivity analyses. Conclusion NHE and HE showed largely shared compression of the sensorimotor-to-transmodal hierarchy, with more selective HE-associated alterations, particularly in temporolimbic regions. These abnormalities were associated with ammonia burden, liver disease severity, and cognitive impairment, supporting altered cortical functional hierarchy as a clinically relevant systems-level phenotype across the cirrhosis–HE spectrum.

item.title: Longitudinal Changes in the Cortico-Reticulospinal Tract Associated with High-Intensity Locomotor Training in Chronic Stroke.
item.description:
Neurorehabilitation and neural repair
Introduction High-intensity locomotor training (HIT) is recommended for improving walking capacity, but treatment responses are variable. Understanding the brain changes underlying responsiveness to training could provide insight into this variability. Emerging evidence suggests upregulation of the contralesional cortico-reticulospinal tract (CRST) may contribute to walking function after stroke. However, it is unclear whether CRST upregulation is supportive or maladaptive, and no studies have examined CRST changes after HIT. This study investigated how CRST and corticospinal tract (CST) strength and laterality reorganize, and their relationship with walking capacity after locomotor HIT. Methods Ten participants with chronic stroke completed a 4-week no-intervention control phase then 4 weeks of HIT. Diffusion MRI and 6-minute walk distance were obtained at weeks 0, 4, and 8. Analysis tested changes in ipsilesional and contralesional CRST and CST strength and laterality. Associations between changes in tract laterality and walking capacity were examined. Results During the treatment phase (vs the control phase), there were significantly greater increases in contralesional CRST strength (1.02 SD [95% CI: 0.25, 1.79]), contralesional CRST laterality (4.44 [2.15, 6.72]), and 6-minute walk distance (33 meters [17, 50]). Walking capacity improvements were associated with changes in CRST laterality (r = 0.77, P = .01), but not CST laterality (r = -0.01, P = 0.98). Discussion Following HIT, increases in contralesional CRST strength and laterality were observed. CRST laterality changes were strongly associated with walking improvements, suggesting an association between contralesional CRST changes and training-related improvements. item.title: Eyes-open resting-state EEG microstate analysis using ratio-normalized parameters across four- and seven-class solutions in healthy controls, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundResting-state EEG microstate analysis indexes large-scale network dynamics, yet the value of ratio-normalized temporal parameters under the eyes-open resting (EOR) condition remains unexplored across the cognitive decline continuum.ObjectiveTo examine whether ratio-normalized microstate parameters from four- and seven-class clustering solutions under EOR differentiate healthy controls (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD).MethodsOne hundred and eighty participants (HC, MCI, and AD; n = 60 each) were recruited from a hospital-based cohort in an elderly Korean population. Resting-state EEG recorded under EOR was analyzed using MICROSTATELAB in EEGLAB. Absolute temporal parameters (duration, occurrence, coverage) and ratio-normalized forms (relative duration, relative occurrence) were compared using ANCOVA with age as covariate, false discovery rate (FDR) correction, and Bonferroni-corrected post-hoc comparisons.ResultsIn the four-class solution, three parameters reached nominal significance, none surviving FDR correction across the full set of 20 tests: coverage of Microstate B (visual network; F(2176) = 3.561, p = 0.030), relative occurrence of Microstate B (F(2176) = 5.281, p = 0.006), and relative occurrence of Microstate E (executive network; F(2176) = 3.816, p = 0.024). MCI showed higher visual and lower executive microstate engagement than AD (p ≤ 0.023); no contrast involving HC was significant. Absolute occurrence parameters were non-significant whereas their ratio-normalized counterparts were significant. The seven-class solution yielded no corrected effects.ConclusionsRatio-normalized EOR microstate parameters distinguished MCI from AD through visual and executive network engagement, with small-to-moderate effects and HC intermediate. The four-class solution outperformed the seven-class solution, contrasting with eyes-closed reports. As these analyses were exploratory and did not survive correction, confirmation in independent cohorts is required.

item.title: Capturing the Attentional Trade-off between Speech Planning and Comprehension.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
In conversation, future speakers often plan speech simultaneously with comprehension, which means that they must divide attentional resources between these processes. In this EEG study, we used responses to linguistic attention probes (i.e., syllable "BA" presented during spoken sentences) to track temporal variations in attention to comprehension. Participants were asked to listen to prerecorded sentences with expected or unexpected sentence-final words. Each sentence was presented twice, once with and once without the attention probe starting 100 msec after the target word onset. Participants saw a picture 50 msec before the target word. Depending on the test block (picture naming or button press), participants either named the picture or pressed the space bar, both after an 850-msec delay. The probes elicited a negative potential approximately 100 msec after probe onset (i.e., an attention probe effect) in all probe conditions. Unexpectedly, neither word expectancy nor speech planning influenced the timing or strength of the attention probe effect. This indicates that expectancy of words in Dutch does not affect the allocation of attention toward these words 100 msec after their onset (i.e., the time of the probe presentation). Interestingly, engaging in speech planning does not seem to divert attentional resources away from comprehension at the moment of probe presentation. These findings imply that listeners are able to effectively distribute their attentional resources between comprehension and speech planning and carry out these processes at the same time. Considering these unexpected findings, using attention probes might not be the best approach to capture variations in temporal attention in dual-task paradigms.

item.title: Distinct Patterns of Syntactic Errors Doubly Dissociate in Chronic Poststroke Aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
The lesion correlates of syntactic deficits in aphasia remain poorly understood. Previous studies have suggested that distinct error types in expressive syntax may be associated with damage to different brain regions, but the specific lesion correlates of these errors have not been fully delineated. To address this gap, we analyzed spontaneous speech samples from individuals with chronic aphasia, categorizing errors into hierarchical (paragrammatic-like) and linearization (agrammatic-like) errors. Lesion-symptom mapping was conducted to identify brain regions associated with these error types. Lesion clusters in the medial superior temporal sulcus and inferior parietal lobe were associated with hierarchical errors, whereas frontal lesions, including those in the inferior and middle frontal lobe, were associated with linearization errors. These results provide support for a two-stage model of syntactic encoding, with distinct neural correlates for hierarchical and linearization processes. Our findings suggest that distinct brain regions contribute to different stages of syntactic encoding. Hierarchical processing seems to be supported by posterior temporal-parietal regions, whereas linearization seems to be supported by frontal regions. These results suggest that the diagnosis and treatment of aphasia could take into account the existence of distinct syntactic production deficits resulting from different patterns of brain damage.

item.title: Theta and High-alpha Phase-locking Dynamics Unveil Face Perception in Ambiguous Stimuli.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Previous studies emphasize phase synchronization as a fundamental mechanism for integrating local features into coherent percepts. We employed a novel paradigm and dynamic graph analysis based on EEG to track neural dynamics associated with perceiving a face (or not) while keeping the stimuli identical. Thirty participants underwent a pretest to establish perceptual thresholds for detecting faces within images overlaid with visual noise. These thresholds were then applied in an EEG experiment with the same task, focusing on images with 50% and 75% detection probabilities. In the high-alpha band, we observed increased coupling (100-275 msec after stimulus onset) between the left and right occipitotemporal electrodes when an ambiguous stimulus was perceived as a face, indicating conscious face perception. The failure to perceive a face resulted in enhanced theta band phase synchronization between bilateral occipitotemporal electrodes and increased high-alpha-band coupling between the left frontal and right occipitotemporal electrodes, which showed face-selective responses. These synchronizations are likely to reflect the continuous gathering of individual bits of facial information rather than signaling the presence or absence of a face percept. Additionally, we identified frontal-occipitotemporal theta-band couplings related to the stimulus's informational content, irrespective of whether the inherent face was perceived. Our findings reveal distinct temporal dynamics in phase synchronization at specific frequencies, indicating a specialized system for face perception during integrated information processing across the frontal and visual cortex, resolving ambiguities.

item.title: Memory Traces Reflect How They Were Last Accessed.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Episodic memories are known to change with each act of retrieval. We hypothesize that accessing semantic knowledge in different ways during episodic retrieval-from unique perceptual features to taxonomic and thematic context-shapes how those memories are subsequently represented during recognition. In this fMRI study, human participants learned novel word-image pairs and underwent re-exposure that required accessing semantic knowledge at one of three different levels: item, category, or theme. Participants then completed a recognition task. Although behavioral memory performance was matched across conditions, neural activity during recognition varied based on prior semantic access history. Recognition patterns could be classified according to prior semantic access in early visual cortex, ventral temporal cortex, and the hippocampus for remembered concepts. A whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed bilateral clusters along the ventral visual stream where semantic access history was decodable. To further characterize how prior semantic access history shaped neural representations during recognition, we tested whether memories accessed at the same semantic level were expressed more similarly or distinctly in the brain. Category-level access increased similarity among items in early visual cortex, whereas item-level access led to more differentiated representations in the visual word form area. Together, these findings show that how we access semantic knowledge during episodic retrieval leaves measurable traces in subsequent neural representations, revealing how semantic-episodic interactions shape memory representations.

item.title: Intracranial Evidence for the Cerebellum's Role in Semantic Processing.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Language impairments in patients with cerebellar damage or dysfunction strongly implicate the cerebellum in language processing but the nature, timing, and specificity of its contributions are unclear. A clinical trial of cerebellar stimulation for motor recovery after middle cerebral artery stroke provided a rare opportunity to record invasive, intracranial local field potential activity from the cerebellar dentate nucleus of eight patients during language processing. Patients performed semantic priming tasks that either discouraged or encouraged semantic predictions. We found evidence for communication between the dentate nucleus and frontal scalp EEG sites in the alpha band when semantic predictions were violated. This did not occur when semantic predictions were fulfilled or when prediction violations were nonlinguistic in nature. This language-specific activity occurred in the N400 window where semantic processing of a visually presented word takes place. These data point to a linguistic feedback function that could help to account for the language deficits observed in diseases and disorders involving the cerebellum.

item.title: Neural Distinctions between Social and Nonsocial Reward Anticipation: An Examination of Activation Magnitude, Representational Patterns, Individual Differences, and Functional Connectivity.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Prevailing theories emphasize a "common neural currency" for social and nonsocial rewards, particularly during reward anticipation. However, direct comparisons of social and nonsocial reward anticipation remain limited, and clinical observations suggest that social reward processing can be selectively disrupted. The present fMRI study directly compared social and nonsocial reward anticipation to test differences in activation magnitude, functional connectivity, multivariate activity patterns, and modulation by individual differences in social reward motivation. Consistent with a "common neural currency" perspective, reward anticipation (collapsed across domains) was associated with increased activation in ventral striatum (VS), anterior insula (AI), dorsal ACC (DACC), and SMA. Furthermore, social reward anticipation did not significantly shape functional connectivity among ventral striatum, AI, DACC, and SMA. However, local activation patterns in AI and SMA reliably discriminated the anticipation of social versus monetary reward. Additional decoding emerged in TPJ, STS, and OFC-regions previously inconsistently linked to social reward anticipation or more commonly associated with later stages of reward processing. Moreover, individual differences in Need to Belong predicted greater ACC (including ventromedial PFC) engagement during social reward anticipation. These findings support the perspective that social and nonsocial reward anticipation share some neural circuitry but are dissociable when local activation patterns and social motivational priorities are considered. The current study recasts our understanding of ways in which social reward anticipation may be distinct and raises an expanded role for brain regions typically associated with reward and/or social processing.

item.title: Transformer Mechanisms Mimic Frontostriatal Gating Operations When Trained on Human Working Memory Tasks.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Working memory (WM) is thought to rely on sophisticated frontostriatal mechanisms for selective gating, supporting updating and readout of information to and from distinct memory "addresses" (neural populations). According to computational models, capacity limitations in WM arise due to challenges in "role addressability": learning to correctly bind items in memory to their respective roles and assigning credit to the corresponding gating operations. However, these conclusions are based on particular assumptions about biological neural networks, and it is unclear whether the principles generalize to other architectures. To address this question, we examine whether similar gating mechanisms emerge in Transformer neural network architectures, which have demonstrated success on tasks requiring executive function-the ability to represent, coordinate, and manage multiple subtasks-yet lack intentionally built-in gating mechanisms. We analyze the mechanisms that emerge within Transformers trained on human WM tasks explicitly designed to place demands on gating. We find that the Transformer's attention mechanism develops role-addressable input and output gating, but only when trained on task distributions that benefit from frontostriatal-like gating mechanisms. Moreover, these gating strategies support enhanced generalization and variable binding and increase the models' effective capacity to store and access multiple items in memory, resembling the constraints found in frontostriatal models. These results suggest that gating mechanisms serve a fundamental computational role in managing role addressability and binding and highlight opportunities for future research on computational similarities between modern artificial intelligence architectures and models of the human brain.

item.title: Slow Oscillations Modulate Overnight Brain Changes in Working Memory Function.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Working memory (WM), the transient storage and manipulation of information, is a cognitive function that can improve with training. Accumulating evidence suggests that sleep, particularly slow oscillations (SOs) that occur during nonrapid eye movement sleep, supports this improvement. Yet, how sleep and SOs in particular relate to neural processes supporting WM remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how WM-related neural activity evolves across nocturnal sleep and how these changes relate to neural processing during SOs. Participants performed a WM task during fMRI before and after sleep, with simultaneous EEG-fMRI capturing neural activity during the first 2.5 hr of sleep. Our results showed significant overnight changes in WM-related activity, characterized by reduced recruitment of the dorsal precuneus during WM encoding/maintenance phases and frontal regions during the retrieval phase of WM. In addition, sleep increased item-specific reinstatement in a sensory processing region during WM. This pattern of results suggests a combined influence of sleep on enhancing sensory reinstatement while reducing potential top-down control (i.e., reduced parietal and frontal activity). Critically, SO-related activity was directly linked to overnight activity changes: Stronger SO activation in the premotor cortex and ventromedial pFC predicted greater overnight reductions in WM-related activity, and multivoxel analyses in the ventral attention network revealed a parallel relationship. These findings suggest that SOs play a critical role in WM function by facilitating the reorganization of WM-related processing.

item.title: Exploring Neural Mechanisms Underlying Error-related Impairments in Active Working Memory Suggests an Adaptive Shielding of Contents during Cognitive Control.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Goal-directed behavior relies on cognitive flexibility-the ability to rapidly adapt ongoing thoughts and behaviors while preserving task-relevant information. The performance monitoring system optimizes such behavior by detecting and evaluating errors, whereas the working memory (WM) system maintains relevant information and protects it from interference. We previously showed that motor errors impaired active WM maintenance (Error-Related Impairment of Active working Memory [ERIAM]; [Wessel, J. R., Jiang, J., & Stolley, J. J. Action errors impair active working memory maintenance. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 151, 1325-1340, 2022]). Here, we investigated the source of ERIAM by tracking the contralateral delay activity (CDA), a neural marker of visual WM maintenance, throughout the error-making process. Forty-two participants maintained visual information in WM while performing a flanker task during the delay period. Consistent with prior results, a significant ERIAM effect occurred. We observed the canonical CDA before flanker task onset, and this CDA declined after the flanker task began. Following the flanker response, however, we observed a sustained contralateral positivity (CDAp). Critically, CDA amplitudes did not differ between motor correct and error trials before the flanker task, ruling out a general performance deficit. The CDA was also unaffected immediately after flanker onset, ruling out a perceptual interference explanation. Neural differences emerged only after the flanker response, supporting a genuinely error-related origin of the ERIAM effect. Importantly, CDAp was larger following correct responses than errors, and greater CDAp modulation predicted a smaller ERIAM effect. On the basis of prior work, we interpret CDAp as reflecting disengagement from WM storage, suggesting a possible adaptive shielding strategy. These findings provide clear evidence regarding the timing of the ERIAM effect and suggestive evidence regarding potential mechanisms underlying error-related interference in active WM maintenance. Future work will help determine the functional significance of CDAp and its relationship to WM storage and cognitive control.

item.title: Visual Perspective Shapes Subjective Experience: Dissociable Parietal Contributions to the Constructive Nature of Memory.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Subjective features of memory are often treated as secondary to the objective content of remembered events. However, growing evidence suggests that these features actively shape how memories are constructed, experienced, and used. Rather than treating visual perspective as a peripheral correlate of subjectivity, this review positions it as a key mechanism that shapes the memory. Because perspective can be flexibly controlled and reliably measured, it offers a unique window into how retrieval goals interact with mental simulation to produce vivid and emotionally resonant recollections. Drawing on behavioral and neuroimaging research, this review shows that visual perspective determines the spatial framing of memory and the emotional and sensory qualities of recollection. Focusing on the posterior parietal cortex, it outlines distinct roles for the angular gyrus (AG) and the precuneus in supporting perspective-dependent retrieval. The AG contributes to the selection and maintenance of a retrieval perspective, integrating perceptual and conceptual features into a coherent scene. In contrast, the precuneus supports spatial transformation and modulates the vividness, emotional tone, and embodied character of recollection, particularly when individuals recall events from a nondominant or shifted perspective. Together, these findings position visual perspective as a central mechanism in the construction of subjectivity. Understanding how perspective shapes the process of remembering provides insight into how memory supports emotion regulation, mental simulation, and the continuity of the self across time.
