item.title: Resting-State and Task-State Dual-Paradigm fNIRS Study Reveals Dynamic Alterations in Brain Network Activity in Alzheimer's Disease With Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms.
item.description:
Psychogeriatrics : the official journal of the Japanese Psychogeriatric Society
Background Alzheimer's disease (AD) frequently presents with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), severely impacting prognosis. The dynamic brain network mechanisms remain unclear, and traditional neuroimaging faces limitations. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a unique approach to explore these mechanisms under natural conditions. Objective To systematically compare brain region activation, signal complexity and network topology in AD patients with and without BPSD using resting-state and verbal fluency task (VFT) fNIRS paradigms. Methods This cross-sectional study enrolled 48 AD patients (24 with BPSD, 24 without) and 25 normal controls (NC). fNIRS recorded hemodynamic changes in the frontal, temporal, parietal and occipital lobes during rest and VFT. Analyses included activation, time-frequency characteristics, functional connectivity and network topology. Partial correlations assessed links between fNIRS metrics and neuropsychological scores. Results In resting state, AD-BPSD showed altered coefficient of variation in left premotor and somatosensory cortices, and elevated information entropy in left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (lDLPFC), versus NC and AD-non-BPSD. Functional connectivity abnormalities emerged between right frontal eye field-left somatosensory cortex, and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC)-left superior temporal gyrus (lSTG) (p < 0.05). During VFT, AD-BPSD had significantly lower lDLPFC and left somatosensory activation versus NC (p < 0.05), but increased signal fluctuation and power in right primary motor cortex (rM1) (p < 0.05), alongside reduced whole-brain clustering coefficient (p = 0.023). Conclusions AD-BPSD was associated with altered brain functional patterns across resting and task states, involving sensorimotor and executive networks as well as altered interhemispheric coordination. These fNIRS-derived alterations provide exploratory evidence of altered brain functional patterns associated with BPSD and warrant further investigation in larger longitudinal studies.

item.title: Six-Month Music Practice Versus Psychomotor Interventions in Mild Cognitive Impairment: Behavioral and Hippocampal Outcomes.
item.description:
Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is characterized by measurable cognitive decline with largely preserved daily functioning and increased risk of dementia. MCI patients may also exhibit sensorimotor and communication impairments, while hippocampal atrophy and altered functional connectivity are prominent neural features associated with further cognitive decline. Evidence from nonpharmacological interventions integrating cognitive challenge, coordinated movement, and emotional engagement remains limited in early-stage MCI. In this pilot intervention study, we examined whether 6 months of intensive musical instrument training versus psychomotor interventions were associated with changes in cognitive and sensorimotor performance, hippocampal gray matter volume, and functional connectivity. Outcomes were compared between randomized MCI groups, with matched healthy controls as reference for test-retest and age-related neural effects. Improvements in global cognition were modest, reaching marginal significance only in the music group, while both interventions were associated with complementary domain-specific cognitive and sensorimotor gains. Hippocampal gray matter volume remained stable across all three groups, whereas hippocampal functional connectivity declined in healthy controls but remained stable in both intervention groups, consistent with possible functional neural maintenance. These preliminary findings suggest that group-based, low-risk music and psychomotor interventions may support cognitive, sensorimotor, and neural functioning in early MCI, warranting further investigation in larger controlled trials.

item.title: Investigation of the Prolonged Impact of Severe Socioeconomic Hardship and Mother's Perceived Social Support on Neurocognitive Development in Young Children in the Rural Ecuadorian Amazon.
item.description:
Developmental science
Children living in conditions of severe socioeconomic (SES) hardship are at elevated risk for neurocognitive delays, yet most developmental neuroscience research has focused on children in high-income, Western populations, limiting our understanding of diverse developmental contexts. This study examined maternal perceived social support as a potential buffer against the stressors associated with SES hardship on child neurocognitive development in a longitudinal sample of Indigenous families in the rural Ecuadorian Amazon. Twenty-eight children (M age = 28.02 months at T1; 57.6 months at T2) participated in the study completing an assessment of early cognitive ability at T1 and an inhibition task while functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measured cortical activation at T2. A three-level linear mixed model revealed a significant interaction between early cognitive ability and maternal perceived social support on functional activation. Specifically, children of mothers with high social support showed no association between early cognitive ability and cortical activation, while those with low support exhibited atypical patterns (hyper- or hypoactivation), suggesting that increased maternal perceived social support may help buffer the risk exposure of chronic stressors associated with SES hardship. These findings underscore the importance of culturally embedded social resources in promoting resilience among children facing cumulative risk. Supporting maternal social networks may be a promising pathway for improving child neurodevelopment in underrepresented, low-resource communities and contributes to more inclusive global models of brain development.

item.title: Perceived Neighborhood Disadvantage Predicts Similarity in Amygdala Representations of Negative and Neutral Images in Early Adolescents.
item.description:
Developmental science
Neighborhood disadvantage encompasses multiple co-occurring adversities, including threat and deprivation, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Applying a dimensional framework to neighborhood contexts may help clarify how distinct features of disadvantage influence brain development. Here, we used representational similarity analysis to investigate associations between adolescents' neural representations of affective valence and neighborhood disadvantage, as measured by caregiver self-report and the Area Deprivation Index (ADI). One hundred and twenty-one adolescents aged 11 to 14 (Mage = 12.81 years old, 52.07% female, 28.93% White non-Hispanic) completed an emotional reactivity fMRI task. Caregiver-reported neighborhood disadvantage was associated with greater representational similarity in right amygdala between negative and neutral images, while no such effect emerged for the ADI. Follow-up analyses examined whether specific dimensions of disadvantage drove these effects. Although our measure did not map cleanly onto threat and deprivation dimensions, factor analyses revealed distinctions between social (e.g., crime, loitering) and physical (e.g., abandoned buildings, walkability) disadvantage-related items; our preliminary findings suggest that the effects of reported overall neighborhood disadvantage may be driven by characteristics of the social environment. No associations between caregiver-reported neighborhood disadvantage or ADI were observed for positive/neutral similarity. These findings provide preliminary evidence that neighborhood disadvantage may impact the amygdala's differentiation of negative and neutral stimuli during early adolescence, supporting the view that neighborhoods are a critical ecological context for development.

item.title: Early Emergence of Cultural Differences in Audiovisual Speech Perception.
item.description:
Developmental science
Integrating auditory and visual cues is a hallmark of human speech perception, yet adults from East Asian backgrounds show less reliance on visual speech than their Western counterparts. The origins of this cultural difference, however, remain unknown. To investigate whether this divergence is established early in infancy, we examined audiovisual integration in 6- to 12-month-old White Canadian (n = 111) and Chinese (n = 115) infants using a novel paradigm measuring their perception of the McGurk effect. Across four experiments, we found a clear developmental divergence: Canadian infants showed a stable McGurk effect from 6 months onward, whereas Chinese infants showed a more protracted developmental trajectory, a cultural pattern that was further highlighted when their integration was challenged by other-race faces. These findings provide the first direct evidence that cultural differences in multisensory speech perception are established within the first year of life, suggesting that the brain's strategy for binding sight and sound is shaped by early experience, with broad implications for theories of language acquisition and developmental science.

item.title: Nucleus Accumbens and Ventral Tegmental Area Functional Connectivity as a Marker of Reward Sensitivity in Infancy.
item.description:
Developmental science
Early functional connectivity within the brain's reward circuitry may provide insight into the developmental origins of individual differences in pleasure and motivation. This study examined resting-state functional connectivity between two key reward-related regions, the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and ventral tegmental area (VTA), in 94 one-month-old infants (58% male; M = 4.84 weeks, SD = 0.86) and its association with later reward-related temperament. Infants completed a resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging scan during natural sleep with a mean of 11.09 (SD = 2.78) min of retained low-motion data. Caregivers reported their infants' temperament at age six months, including high- and low-intensity pleasure as indicators of individual differences relevant to reward sensitivity. Positive resting-state functional connectivity between the NAc and VTA was present in early infancy (Cohen's d = 0.44, 95% CI [0.22, 0.65]), p < 0.001). Less positive NAc-VTA connectivity was associated with greater high-intensity pleasure at six months (β = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.54, -0.10], p = 0.004), indicating that infants with stronger connectivity between these regions exhibited less enjoyment of highly stimulating, energetic activities. NAc-VTA connectivity was not associated with low-intensity pleasure (β = -0.01, 95% CI [-0.24, 0.21], p = 0.908). These findings suggest that early variation in mesolimbic connectivity may serve as a marker of emerging individual differences in reward responsiveness, with implications for understanding affective development in infancy.

item.title: Computation or Weight Adaptation? Rethinking the Role of Plasticity in Learning.
item.description:
Cognitive science
The human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. The traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). In this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (LLMs), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. We focus on statistical learning paradigms. These require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. LLMs can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, even though these structures carry no semantic content and lie far from the natural language distribution on which the models were trained. Our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. Furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain.

item.title: Lexico-Semantic and Morphosyntactic Skills in Individuals With Parkinson's Disease: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
International journal of language & communication disorders
Purpose This scoping review examines lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic skills in English-speaking individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD) using behavioral and neuroimaging data to inform clinical assessment and intervention. Method Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, observational case-control studies published between 2004 and 2024 were retrieved from PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus and ERIC. Thirty-nine studies met inclusion criteria. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for Case-Control Studies. Results Lexico-semantic impairments in PD are characterized by deficits in semantic fluency, action-verb retrieval, and figurative-language processing, particularly under higher cognitive load. Individuals with PD show reduced efficiency in lexical access, difficulty shifting between semantic categories, and weaker inhibition of competing meanings. Morphosyntactic studies similarly report slower processing and lower accuracy for syntactically complex sentences. Conclusion Linguistic impairments in PD are best understood as a dynamic interaction between linguistic demands and domain-general cognitive resources, emerging most clearly under conditions of increased cognitive load. This pattern positions language as a sensitive indicator of broader cognitive vulnerability within the communication profile of PD, with direct implications for assessment and clinical practice. What this paper adds What is already known on the subject Language impairments are a well-recognized non-motor feature of PD and can significantly affect communication and quality of life. Previous studies have reported lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic difficulties in PD, but findings are scattered across heterogeneous tasks and study designs, with no synthesis examining these domains together. What this study adds to the existing knowledge This scoping review synthesizes evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging studies and shows that language difficulties in PD are most consistently observed under conditions of increased cognitive or processing demand, particularly in high-load contexts. Lexico-semantic impairments emerge reliably in such high-load contexts, while morphosyntactic difficulties appear to reflect vulnerability to processing demands rather than a generalized grammatical deficit. The review also demonstrates that methodological variability, such as cognitive screening practices, influences how language abilities are characterized across studies. What are the potential or clinical implications of this work? Language impairments affecting lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic processing constitute a meaningful component of the communication profile in PD and should be considered alongside speech and voice symptoms in clinical assessment. Incorporating cognitive-linguistic evaluation may support a more comprehensive understanding of communication difficulties in individuals with PD.
